reading.body:
Defense AI procurement is documented in free federal databases, SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial entry point and subscription analysts layered on top.

The free sources are the primary record. SAM.gov lists solicitations and awards, USAspending carries every federal award, and FPDS records contract actions and vendor performance at the transaction level. DIU is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini builds decision science on that record, and Silicon Valley Defense Group maps the commercial entrants.

The programs of record are decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing, the AI applications the sector tracks. Tracking them through procurement data shows actual spending and vendor capability, not just announcements. What the data does not show is compute demand, building capacity, or power requirements, none of those appear in these sources. Government AI labs are catalogued separately, not here.

summary: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing are the programs of record; DIU is the commercial on-ramp. Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
The material assembled here does not include an official adoption measurement for defense, so no measured rate of AI use can be reported for the sector. What the sources do show is the machinery around adoption: where solicitations are published, where awards are recorded, which organizations act as gateways for commercial technology, and which analysts supply context. There is also no ROI evidence in these excerpts, from any source, so nothing can be said about returns on defense AI spending.

The procurement record is the backbone. Per SAM.gov, the site is the government's system of record for contract opportunities, awards, and subcontract reports, and it notes that following revisions to the ISR eligibility logic within the Subcontracting Plan Reporting system on June 9, 2026, contractors might observe an increased volume of contracts and subcontracts in their Eligible Workspace. SAM.gov also states that the FPDS.gov ezSearch feature has been retired and that all contract award searches should be conducted in SAM.gov, with the FPDS.gov ATOM Feed to be retired later in FY 2026. The General Services Administration has retired the Electronic Subcontracting Reporting System, with subcontracting reporting capabilities now available in SAM.gov, according to the FPDS page. FPDS itself, per that page, records contract actions at the transaction level, and federal users manage contract award records with legacy FPDS credentials. USAspending.gov appears in the material only as a destination, with the curated note that every federal award is downloadable and that AI-related contract spending traces there on the Federal Procurement Data System feed.

The Defense Innovation Unit is described as the Department's innovation pointman, with a stated mission to convert entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power, and the curated note places it as where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini is described as building on that record, with its platform layer transforming activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that proactively forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources. The curated description adds that Govini tracks procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy and publishes public scorecards on critical-technology spending. The site's own summary of this page frames the subject as decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing as programs of record, with DIU as the commercial on-ramp.

For analysis rather than transaction data, Janes describes itself as a source of open source defence and security intelligence, using vetted on-the-ground and industry specialists as human sensors, verifying every data point against vetted sources, and peer reviewing final content. Janes states it maintains the largest global dataset of its type and that its validated data and analysis inform the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Forecast International is named in the curated points as a long-running defense analysis provider covering contractors, programs, and procurement forecasts, though no page from that organization appears in the excerpts, so nothing further can be drawn from it here. The Silicon Valley Defense Group is described in the curated points as a nonprofit monitoring commercial tech, private capital, and national security and mapping companies driving AI adoption in the DoD space, but the text harvested from its page does not describe that work, so that description stands uncorroborated by the excerpt.

On the government research side, the Government Labs page catalogues two individually verified organizations. It describes the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi as operating under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and having published frontier open models, and Shanghai AI Laboratory as a state-established Chinese research institution backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government. The page's point is structural: state-funded labs carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, and both institutions can in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy into this sector, the practical takeaway from these sources is procedural rather than financial. The free federal record, SAM.gov, FPDS, and USAspending, is the first place to look, and it is currently in transition, with search consolidated into SAM.gov and the FPDS ATOM Feed scheduled for retirement later in FY 2026. DIU is the named commercial on-ramp, and subscription analysts such as Janes supply the validated context that the raw award data does not. SAM.gov also notes that the system contains Controlled Unclassified Information and that handling must follow 32 CFR Part 2002 and GSA Order CIO 2103.2, which is the clearest compliance obligation stated anywhere in this material. Nothing in these excerpts reports what defense AI deployments have returned, so any claim about ROI would have to come from somewhere other than these sources.

https://www.svdg.org/.brief: The page presents Motiv, an agency run by Andrej Schindler and Jonas von der Gathen that describes itself as an "Agentur für Zukunftspotenziale", placing creative people with values-oriented companies. It says it connects people and companies, accompanies individual development and creates space for future perspectives, driven by curiosity about people and how organisations evolve. Companies are described as grown, unique organisms whose sense of purpose and urge to develop are their driving forces, and the agency says its aim is to place people who bring both professional expertise and the ability to connect with a company's purpose. It states that it works with companies holding social and ecological values and seeks long-term working relationships, and that it sees people as developing beings whose individual potential it tries to recognise at the right moment for a career step. The page also invites readers to register for a quarterly newsletter with open positions, accounts of company visits and interviews.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The World of AI lists two individually verified government labs, each carrying a classification note with the source that decided it and the date that source was last read. It describes Shanghai AI Laboratory as a state-established Chinese research institution backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government, while placing the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi under that emirate's Advanced Technology Research Council and crediting it with published frontier open models. The page argues that state-funded labs hold a distinct position because they carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, which it says shapes what they build and why. It adds that both institutions can in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially. The site states that each entry was classified one at a time against a document the organisation published about itself, rather than by keyword, model or inheritance from a parent company.
